Quillen; James Blake Quillen; Carolyn Quillen; and Pfluger Family Limited Partnership

(collectively, the “N12/P1 Intervenors”) and file this Initial Post-Hearing Brief (this “Brief”) for

upon which Link P1 would be constructed2 and Pfluger Family Limited Partnership owns real

constructed upon the real property owned by KLM Griffin Ranch, L.P.4

                              I.      Procedural History and Introduction

        On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA

Transmission Services Corporation (“LCRA”) (collectively, “Applicants”) filed a joint Standard

Application for a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for a Proposed Transmission Line (the

“Application”) for the Bell County East Switch – Big Hill Substation 765 kilovolt (“kV”)

transmission line project in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch,

Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties, Texas (the

“Proposed Transmission Line”). The Application details the construction of the Proposed

Transmission Line, which consists of a new 765-kV single-circuit transmission line between

approximately 214 to 248 miles long and built on steel lattice tower structures 155 to 198 feet tall,

        In the Application, of the 1,246 routes Applicants considered, Applicants recommended

Route 894 as the route that “best meets” the requirements of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)–(D) and

TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).7 Subsequently, the Public Utility Commission (the “PUC”) Staff

Alternatively, N12/P1 Intervenors file this Brief in support of any route not utilizing Links N12,

                                              II.      Jurisdiction

        The PUC has jurisdiction over this matter under PURA §§ 14.001,32.001, 37.053, and

37.056, and 16 TAC § 25.101. The State Office of Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”) has

jurisdiction over this proceeding under Texas Government Code § 2003.049 and PURA § 14.053.

After receiving a substantial number of requests to intervene in this action, the matter was referred

to SOAH. The hearing on the merits for this matter was conducted in Austin, Texas at the J.J.

Pickle Research Campus for five (5) days from June 8, 2026 to June 12, 2026.

                               III.     Legal Standard for Route Selection

        The over-arching issue in this matter is which Proposed Transmission Line route is the best

route when considering and weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and TAC

community values; (5) recreational and park areas; (6) historical and aesthetic values;

(7) environmental integrity; (8) the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to

consumers in the area if the certificate is granted; (9) engineering constraints; (10) costs and length;

(10) paralleling of existing compatible rights-of-way; (11) paralleling of property lines or other

natural or cultural features; and (12) conformance with the policy of prudent avoidance

(collectively, the “Factors”).9 While no single Factor controls or is dispositive, the PUC is directed

to reasonably consider the various Factors and their impact.10 Length, cost, and habitable structures

either Route 894 or Route 487 should be selected by the PUC for the construction of the Proposed

Transmission Line.12 The record further makes clear that when all Factors are weighed, Routes

A.      Community Values

        While the term “community values” is included as a factor for consideration under PURA

§ 37.056(c)(4)(A), the term is not formally defined by statute or in the PUC’s rules. In the past, the

PUC has construed the term to mean “a shared appreciation of an area or other natural resource by

a national, regional, or local community.”14 A transmission line may adversely affect “community

values” when the transmission line significantly alters the use, enjoyment, or intrinsic value

attached to an important area or resource by the community.15 Given the distance, geographic

diversity, difference in land use, and varying population densities across the Proposed

Transmission Line, it is not unsurprising that community values may differ in various parts of the

study area. In this case, Applicants and PUC Staff properly considered community values in

recommending Route 894 and Route 487, respectively.

        In order to “help ensure that the values and concerns of the affected communities are

adequately identified and considered,”16 Applicants held a series of open house meetings in June

of 2025 at locations in Salado, Lampasas, and Menard, Texas.17 Applicants sent written notices

informing people of the Proposed Transmission Line and the scheduled public open house

meetings to 2,809 potentially-affected landowners,18 78 public agencies and officials,19 and eight

        From these meetings and questionaries, Applicants were able to identify thirteen (13)

         2. Route 392 Does Not Reasonably Accommodate Community Values

        Route 392, which utilizes Links N12 and P1, does not reflect the values of the affected

communities in the same way that Routes 894 and 487 do. Route 392 is more expensive,29 longer,

and contains significantly more habitable structures than Route 894 and Route 487.30

        Specifically, Route 392 (1) is 5.85 miles longer than Route 89431 and 7.52 miles longer

than Route 487,32 (2) parallels 9.56 fewer miles of compatible rights-of-way than Route 89433 and

21.5 fewer miles of compatible rights-of-way than Route 487,34 (3) crosses 51 more habitable

structures than Route 89435 and 40 more habitable structures than Route 487, (4) contains 33 more

stream crossings than Route 894 and 42 more stream crossings than Route 487, and (5) affects 49

more recorded cultural resources when compared to Route 894 and 43 more when compared to

Route 487.36 Accordingly, Route 392 intensifies, rather than mitigates, the concerns raised by the

public when compared to Routes 894 and 487.

        The evidence is clear that Route 392 would be contrary to the community values outlined

in PURA § 37.056(c) and the criteria emphasized by the public during and after Applicants’ public

meetings.

         4. Links N12, O1, and P1 Do Not Reasonably Accommodate Community Values

        Oncor confirmed that the historic significance of a piece of property is a relevant

consideration when looking at the community values in a particular area.42 Commissioner Barry

Smitherman, previous chairman of the PUC, further agreed that “where there is careful and

continuous stewardship of land that is and/or will be part of multi-generational family legacies, we

should seek to avoid disturbing that [land].”43

        The Pfluger properties located along Links N12 and P1 have been in Mr. Pfluger’s family

for approximately 100 years and 75 years, respectively.44 The Cave Springs Ranch located along

Link P1 has been ranched by the Quillen family for seven (7) generations, with Carolyn Quillen

inheriting her interest in the land from her grandmother who was born on the ranch in 1899.45 The

Henderson Ranch located along Link P1 has been in the Quillen family for over 70 years.46 Finally,

the Kickapoo Springs Ranch along Links N12, O1, and P1 was established in 1880.47 Accordingly,

the historic, family legacy properties owned by N12/P1 Intervenors are relevant when considering

community values in the southern portions of Concho, Tom Green, and Schleicher Counties.

        The Pfluger property located in Concho County (the “Concho County Property”) affected

by Link N12 is approximately 2,700 acres and the property located in Tom Green County (the

“Tom Green County Property”) affected by Link P1 is approximately 7,120 acres (collectively,

the “Properties” in this section).48 The Properties have been used for hunting wildlife and raising

        The Cave Springs Ranch, located along Link P1, is part of the Quillen family’s long-

The Cave Springs Ranch, unsurprisingly, contains a well-known cave with natural springs and

deep water draws that would be directly crossed by Link P1.57 Natural springs, and even just

natural groundwater in general, are extremely hard to come by in West Texas.58 The cave in

particular is locally famous for its reputation as a hideout for the Ketchum Brothers and their gang

as well as the Kickapoo Indians.59 Many arrowheads have been found in and around the cave.60

Constructing the Proposed Transmission Line across the cave is concerning as the depth and size

         Ms. Quillen, managing partner of the Quillen Family Partnership, Ltd., is a founding

member and officer of the Edwards Plateau Alliance (the “Alliance”), which is made up of

community members and landowners in Tom Green, Menard, Concho, Schleicher, and other

surrounding counties who want to protect and preserve the unique nature of the Edwards Plateau.62

The Edwards Plateau Alliance is dedicated to educating and empowering local Texas communities

regarding the true impact of large-scale energy projects on our natural resources, wildlife habitats,

rural heritage, and Edwards Plateau landforms.63 The members making up the Alliance envision a

future where the Edwards Plateau region of Texas thrives with preserved natural beauty and the

natural resources benefit local residents for generations to come.64 The mere existence of the

Alliance indicates the level of importance to the community that the natural beauty and landforms

in this this area be preserved. The Alliance is opposed to the Proposed Transmission Line.65

        The Henderson Ranch, located along Link P1, was settled by the Henderson family, who

began ranching in the region around 1880.66 The Quillen family purchased this piece of West Texas
